title: EZEKIEL EXPOSED THE BEDROOMS OF JERUSALEM—AND THE LAST WORD WASN’T SEX
paragraphs: EZEKIEL EXPOSED THE BEDROOMS OF JERUSALEM—AND THE LAST WORD WASN’T SEX

Men were taking their fathers’ wives, defiling daughters-in-law, violating sisters, betraying neighbors—and then God revealed the terrifying root beneath it all: “You have forgotten Me.” — Ezekiel 22:10–12
There are passages in the Bible people read slowly because they are beautiful.
And then there are passages people read slowly because they cannot believe God actually allowed those words onto the page.
This is not a comfortable chapter.
It does not smell like polished church pews and Sunday morning perfume.
It smells like a city rotting behind closed doors.
And behind doors that should have been safe...
Men were crossing lines so dark that thousands of years later the accusations still make a reader recoil.
And God told Ezekiel to expose it.
Because sometimes the most frightening thing about sin is not what it looks like when it begins.
It is what it becomes when nobody repents.
Listen to the Hebrew of Ezekiel 22:10:
Literally, the language speaks of “uncovering a father’s nakedness.”
Ezekiel is drawing from the sexual holiness laws already given to Israel. Leviticus 18:8 says:
“עֶרְוַת אֵשֶׁת־אָבִיךָ לֹא תְגַלֵּה עֶרְוַת אָבִיךָ הִוא”
“The nakedness of your father’s wife you shall not uncover; it is your father’s nakedness.”

Ezekiel 22:10 does not contain the words “father’s wife” in precisely the same expanded form as Leviticus 18:8. But the Torah itself explains the expression: violating the sexual boundary surrounding a father’s wife was described as uncovering the father’s nakedness.
This is why the accusation has historically been understood as incestuous sexual violation involving the father’s wife or bed.
And Ezekiel is nowhere near finished.
“וְאִישׁ אֶת־אֵשֶׁת רֵעֵהוּ עָשָׂה תּוֹעֵבָה וְאִישׁ אֶת־כַּלָּתוֹ טִמֵּא בְזִמָּה וְאִישׁ אֶת־אֲחֹתוֹ בַת־אָבִיו עִנָּה־בָךְ”
The accusations come one after another.
A man with his neighbor’s wife.
Another violating his sister—his father’s daughter.
The ancient Greek Septuagint preserves the horror with similarly severe language:
“ἕκαστος τὴν γυναῖκα τοῦ πλησίον αὐτοῦ ἠνομοῦσαν ... καὶ ἕκαστος τὴν νύμφην αὐτοῦ ἐμίαινεν ... καὶ ἕκαστος τὴν ἀδελφὴν αὐτοῦ θυγατέρα τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτοῦ ἐταπείνουν ἐν σοί.”
This was not Ezekiel exaggerating to generate attention.
And that distinction matters because we live in an age where scandal has become entertainment.
Someone falls and everybody reaches for a phone.
A marriage collapses and strangers want screenshots.
A pastor sins and suddenly everyone becomes a detective.
A celebrity is exposed and millions gather around the digital wreckage.
Gossip exposes another person so we can feel superior.
God exposes sin so sinners will understand what rebellion has done.
And if you read Ezekiel 22 only to stare at those people, you may completely miss the blade of the passage turning toward us.
Because sexual depravity was not the only charge.
Before Ezekiel ever reaches the bedroom, he talks about bloodshed.
He talks about leaders abusing power.
He talks about dishonoring fathers and mothers.
He talks about mistreating orphans and widows.
He talks about despising what God calls holy.
The chapter refuses to let respectable sinners stand at a safe distance from scandalous sinners.
and the sins that fit comfortably inside respectable clothing.
God does not play that game.
Ezekiel exposes an entire culture whose relationship with God had disintegrated so badly that human beings themselves were becoming objects to exploit.
And suddenly the connection becomes painfully clear.
When God disappears from the center of human life, people eventually stop looking sacred too.
A vulnerable person becomes an easy target.
But then Ezekiel says something more terrifying than almost anything else in the chapter.
God identifies something underneath it all.
Maybe that is the line we were supposed to be afraid of.
Because most people reading this have probably never committed the specific incestuous sins Ezekiel describes.
You can remember Christian vocabulary and forget Christ.
You can remember Sunday and forget Christ on Monday.
You can remember worship lyrics while forgetting the One being worshiped.
You can post Scripture and secretly live as though God cannot see your browser history.
You can tell everyone, “God is good,” while nurturing something inside you that God has repeatedly told you to surrender.
You can know theology and forget God.
You can serve in ministry and forget God.
You can preach and forget God.
You can sing and forget God.
You can build a Christian-looking life around the absence of intimate obedience to Christ.
That may be one of the most terrifying possibilities in religion.
And maybe somebody reading this just became uncomfortable.
Not because Ezekiel exposed ancient Jerusalem.
Because the Holy Spirit touched a locked room inside you.
Something you keep promising will be the last time.
The relationship you know is wrong.
The messages your spouse would be devastated to read.
The bitterness you have baptized as discernment.
The person you refuse to forgive.
The secret appetite you feed whenever loneliness gets loud.
The version of yourself everybody applauds...
and the version only God sees.
Conviction is not an invitation to despair.
It is an invitation to stop hiding.
The Gospel does not tell us that sin is harmless.
The Gospel tells us sin is so serious that the Son of God went to a cross to save sinners from it.
Jesus did not die so we could rename darkness.
He died to rescue us from darkness.
He did not shed His blood so we could make peace with the chains He came to break.
Grace is not God looking at evil and shrugging.
Grace is God doing for guilty sinners what guilty sinners could never do for themselves.
And this is where Ezekiel's nightmare drives us toward the breathtaking necessity of Jesus Christ.
Centuries after Ezekiel described sexual corruption in Jerusalem, Paul wrote to another deeply troubled community in Corinth.
He named sexual immorality, idolatry, adultery, greed, drunkenness, reviling and swindling among sins incompatible with inheriting God's kingdom when they characterize an unrepentant life.
Then comes one of the most beautiful turns in Scripture.
Not because they had never been guilty.
Paul continues by saying they had been washed, sanctified and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God (1 Corinthians 6:9–11).
Some of the people sitting in the Corinthian church had histories.
And the Gospel did not require them to pretend those histories never happened.
The Gospel gave those histories a new ending.
Not good people congratulating themselves for avoiding scandal.
Dead people being made alive in Christ.
Sinners becoming saints—not because sin suddenly became acceptable, but because Jesus Christ became their Savior and Lord.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
Agreeing with God about what He calls sin.
Running toward Christ instead of hiding from Him.
“If people knew what I did, they would never look at me the same.”
You are not informing Christ when you confess.
You are surrendering what He already sees.
The cross happened with full knowledge of human depravity.
Christ was not naïve about the people He came to save.
Romans says that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and that justification comes by God's grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus (Romans 3:23–24).
Grace does not mean consequences magically disappear.
Some sins leave wounds requiring years of healing.
Criminal abuse should not be hidden behind religious language; victims deserve protection, truth, justice and appropriate lawful intervention.
Forgiveness must never become a weapon for protecting abusers.
Repentance does not mean demanding immediate trust from the people you wounded.
A repentant heart stops protecting the sin and starts submitting to truth.
That matters especially when reading Ezekiel 22 because some of the language describes violation, exploitation and abuse—not merely private consensual indiscretion.
In fact, the chapter proves He does.
The blood that had been spilled mattered.
God's holiness is not cold perfection detached from human suffering.
His holiness means evil does not receive the final word.
That is where the theme of Gospel Warrior becomes more than a slogan.
Not by rewriting evil into something good.
Jesus rewrites everything by taking people whose stories appeared permanently chained to guilt and giving them something they could never manufacture:
The Corinthian believers carried histories Paul was unafraid to name.
The Gospel does not say your scandal was imaginary.
It says your scandal does not have to be your final identity.
Your worst night does not outrank the blood of Christ.
Your worst decision is not more powerful than His mercy.
Your shame cannot crucify Jesus a second time and prove His first sacrifice insufficient.
But grace must never become permission to continue deliberately embracing what nailed Christ to the cross.
Jesus saves us from sin, not merely from embarrassment about sin.
So maybe this article did not reach you accidentally.
Maybe you started reading because the title shocked you.
But now you realize the article was never merely about what those men were doing thousands of years ago.
It became about the door inside your own heart you hoped nobody would open.
God already knows what is behind it.
Not after you finally defeat everything yourself.
Ask for help where help is needed.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to describe your private sin publicly.
Someone reading the comments may need your testimony more than you realize.
Maybe they think Christians are people who never broke.
Show them Christians are people who know where broken sinners can go.
Because somebody on your Facebook friends list may be quietly drowning in shame while smiling in every photograph.
Someone may believe God wants nothing to do with them anymore.
Someone may be one confession away from finally seeking help.
Someone may need to discover tonight that conviction is not God inviting them to run away—it may be mercy calling them home.

There may come a night when temptation returns, shame starts speaking, or somebody you love confesses something devastating and you need to remember the difference between excusing sin and proclaiming grace.
Invite the friend who says they no longer believe.
The Gospel is not afraid of complicated people.
Jesus has been rescuing complicated people for a very long time.

Scripture says giving should come from the heart rather than from compulsion, because “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). Scripture also recognizes the legitimacy of materially supporting Gospel ministry and those laboring to spread God's Word (1 Corinthians 9:14; Philippians 4:15–18).
And there is another reason your support reaches beyond a single article.
Someone somewhere may have no Christian bookstore nearby.
Yet a biblical resource placed freely within reach can become something God uses in their discipleship.
A discipleship resource for someone newly following Jesus.
A biblical message arriving at exactly the moment someone was preparing to surrender to temptation.
But the deepest reason to support Gospel work is not merchandise.
A share can cross a boundary money cannot.
It can reach the cousin you rarely speak to.
The believer secretly trapped in sexual sin.
The person convinced they have gone too far for Jesus.
Never underestimate what God can do with truth placed in front of the right person at the right moment.
Christ already settled the price of our redemption with something infinitely more precious than money.
Support the work because you love Jesus.
Support it because you value biblical truth.
Support it because you want more people reached.
Support it because generosity can become worship when it rises from a surrendered heart.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with being saved.
And that brings us back to Jerusalem.
But thousands of years later, standing on this side of Calvary, we know something Ezekiel's accusations make desperately necessary.
The Judge against whom humanity has sinned is the God who sent His Son to save sinners.
At the cross, justice was not mocked.
And from the empty tomb came the announcement that death itself does not get the last word over those who belong to Him.
You may have a chapter you wish could be torn from your life.
Jesus does not need you to lie about that chapter.
You may carry memories that still make your stomach tighten.
Make what restitution you rightly can.
You may have been the one violated rather than the one violating.
The shame belongs to the evil committed against you, not to your worth before God.
You are not invisible in Ezekiel's world.
The God who thundered against exploitation is not indifferent to your tears.
And maybe that is what somebody needed tonight.
Not another Christian pretending Christians never fall.
The One who tells the truth about sin without abandoning repentant sinners to despair.
The One who can take a confession and begin a restoration.
The One who can enter the chapter you thought ruined the entire book.
What have I been asking Jesus to forgive while secretly planning to keep?
Because somewhere tonight, somebody thinks their scandal is the end of their story.
Make sure they hear the Gospel before shame writes the final sentence.
The sin God exposes is never more powerful than the Savior to whom repentance runs.
